title: New York Banned ICE Contracts. Pro-ICE Sheriffs Could Stand in the Way.
author: Felipe De La Hoz
content:
_This story is_  _part of Bolts’ series on sheriff_ s _in the run-up to the
midterms; read more on  [Maryland](https://boltsmag.org/frederick-county-
immigration-enforcement-sheriff-chuck-jenkins/), [North
Carolina](https://boltsmag.org/alamance-county-sheriff-terry-johnson-shannon-
long/), [Washington](https://boltsmag.org/constitutional-sheriff-klickitat-
county-washington/), and [Wisconsin](https://boltsmag.org/wisconsin-sheriff-
races-immigration-sauk-winnebago/)._

  
When New York legislators approved the state budget earlier this year, they
[folded in](https://nysfocus.com/2026/05/22/hochul-budget-new-york-
immigration-protections-collaboration-deal) legislation [to
protect](https://boltsmag.org/new-york-leaders-prepare-for-ice-hochul-
mamdani/) immigrant communities from President Donald Trump’s aggressive
crackdown. The legislation, which bars localities from contracting with
federal immigration agencies, was a victory for immigrants’ rights advocates
but they knew it was only part of the battle; ensuring compliance would be
crucial to actually reducing ICE’s presence in the state.

The most visible sort of cooperation that New York barred was participation in
the 287(g) program, which effectively deputizes local law enforcement to carry
out some of the functions of immigration agents. But lawmakers also restricted
county detention contracts, which allow ICE to hold detainees in local jails
in exchange for federal money—a practice [that
exploded](https://nysfocus.com/2025/09/16/ice-detentions-new-york-county-
jails) last year as ICE arrests surged.

Orange County, a populous community some 30 miles northwest of New York City
whose jail had become a sort of waystation in ICE’s national detention
network, has quickly become a test of the law’s aftermath.

The jail is run by Sheriff Paul Arteta, a Republican who is holding ICE
detainees there in accordance with a contract that the county first [entered
into in 2008](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/2157390-orange-county-
ny-igsa-contract/?mode=document), and that has long drawn scrutiny due to [the
dismal conditions immigrants
have](https://documentedny.com/2018/11/29/assembly-members-slam-orange-county-
jail-over-immigrant-detention-conditions/) endured. The new state law is
forcing Orange County to terminate this relationship, though so far the
transfer of immigrant detainees out of the jail has been opaque.

Arteta has [resisted](https://midhudsonnews.com/2026/09/16/sheriffs-seek-
pause-on-albany-ban-on-ice-partnerships/) the law, joining a group of law
enforcement officials to [sue over its
implementation](https://www.recordonline.com/story/news/local/2026/08/27/orange-
county-claims-ny-ice-ban-strips-local-powers-critical-
funding/91489699007/?gnt-cfr=1&gca-cat=p&gca-uir=false&gca-
epti=z116301p003050c003050e006330v116301&gca-ft=109&gca-ds=sophi) in late
August. The lawsuit also includes sheriffs in counties [like
Broome](https://boltsmag.org/prosecutor-and-sheriff-elections-in-
november-2026-preview/#new-york) that were in the 287(g) program. Now, Arteta
and other Republicans are railing against the law as the midterm elections
approach. Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, the GOP nominee for governor
who [had joined](https://www.cityandstateny.com/policy/2025/03/nassau-enters-
controversial-task-force-agreement-ice/403817/) 287(g) last year, is
[attacking](https://www.facebook.com/BruceBlakemanNewYorkFirst/posts/hochul-
is-ending-ice-cooperation-and-making-new-york-less-safe-i-stand-with-
law-/1618210953644714/) Governor Kathy Hochul for “making New York less safe.”

ICE cooperation is also an issue in the sheriff’s race between Arteta and
Democratic challenger Bernie Rivers, who has criticized the county’s ties with
the agency. Arteta says no longer renting space to ICE in the local jail [will
hurt](https://www.wamc.org/2026-09-16/orange-county-sheriff-says-local-cops-
local-crimes-will-cost-county-10-million) the county budget.

Immigrants’ rights groups, meanwhile, say they’re focused on the health and
safety of detainees in Orange County. This summer, Dignity Not Detention, a
statewide coalition that has long advocated for the termination of ICE
contracts, began preparing people held in Orange County for transfers and
teaching them their rights, said Kate Johnson-Powers, post-release manager at
Envision Freedom Fund, an organization that supports immigrants. “But of
course, none of us knew what to expect, besides the legal definitions.”

* * *

An earlier generation of debates over county detention contracts with
ICE—including in neighboring New Jersey during the first Trump
administration—pitted advocates who wanted local jails to stop holding people
for ICE against people who were typically their allies, [immigration public
defenders](https://www.bronxdefenders.org/nyifup-statement-about-hudson-
countys-contract-with-ice/) and families of those detained. The latter pointed
out that cancelling the contracts would not necessarily mean anyone would be
released from detention, but instead merely [moved
elsewhere](https://newjerseymonitor.com/2021/11/17/bergen-county-jail-
transfers-last-ice-detainees-to-facility-300-miles-away/), probably much
further away in southern states [like
Louisiana](https://boltsmag.org/louisiana-immigration-detention-habeas-
crisis/).

But during the second Trump administration, constant transfers have been [the
norm](https://www.opb.org/article/2026/03/13/map-ice-detainees-transferred-
often-flown-farther/) for ICE.

Observers of the Orange County jail, or OCJ, told _Bolts_ that, starting in
early 2025, it became increasingly routine for federal authorities to bring
people to Orange County after arresting them in New York City or upstate, but
then quickly transfer them out of state while bringing in people from far
away.

“We have seen our clients at OCJ get transferred sometimes in batches,
sometimes just individually across the country multiple times,” said Rosa
Cohen-Cruz, immigration policy director at the Bronx Defenders. “Often during
those processes they lose medication, they’ll get to their new facility and
won’t have commissary, so won't be able to make a phone call, they lose
property in the transfer.”

The agency is under no legal obligation to hold people near where they were
detained or where their attorneys are.

Ben McCoubrey, data and advocacy manager at Envision, has tracked detainees at
OCJ using data obtained by the [Deportation Data
Project](https://app.deportationdata.org/?agency=ice&dataset=detention-
stints&tab=chart&s=eJxNjtFKw0AURH-
lzPMGkhQU7ltQEUVSEH2QUpaYbtvVzb1hc1MsJf8u29LSxzlzYOaIPWhuMGijILQystpvkV_PAwzUdw6ETlh3MNg6AWHTtD54PSQQexCsZWFnLQy6lMu8vMvy-
ywvYPAXQcuEyqzIz-jSF3OsDDY-
qIsD6Ag99GluG2XsYdAK_4BQ1Y8p7HxYR8eg5VWMY3AnL4CwdupYvbC9OSjpj2cY7JskLd6r-vlp9rD4rD
--Zq_Vyxum1TT9A0epToY) as well as Envision’s own information on detainees it’s
in touch with. He told _Bolts_ that before the start of the second Trump
administration, the jail consistently had 40 to 50 ICE detainees.

He, too, stressed that federal authorities have been cycling people in and out
of OCJ quickly. “They started booking tons of people in, transferring a ton of
people out to make space, and just continued,” he said. In recent months, the
immigrant population has hit a high of around 120 at once, many either recent
arrests, recently transferred in, or on their way out.

“I’ve seen guys come in one night, and the next day they’re shipped out,” said
Samuel, a former ICE detainee who spent roughly seven months at OCJ, through
the end of August (his name was changed to protect his identity, as he has an
active immigration case).

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Orange-County-Jail-
Exterior-Goshen-NY-e1792591650327.webp)The sign outside the Orange County Jail
in Goshen, New York (photo by Kimberly Izar, courtesy of Radio Catskill).  

While Samuel was able to win release through a habeas petition, most of his
fellow detainees have not. “This guy I know got sent to Texas, he got sent
with another guy then came back from Texas, then went to Louisiana, came back
from Louisiana,” he said. “They don’t explain nothing to you. Besides what
your lawyer explained to you and the [immigration judge] explained to you,
whether you get denied or post bond, that’s the only information you get to
know.”

From his time in the OCJ, he described how corrections personnel kept
shortening the time that they would notify detainees that they would be
transferred after some started refusing and trying to barricade themselves
inside their cells.

Other detainees backed up this account of cyclical transfers. “They’ll take
people over to go suffer over there and then bring them back to Orange County,
from Pennsylvania and Louisiana,” said Mateo (also a pseudonym), a detainee
who was picked up by ICE while going to work in November 2025 and held until
this July.

New York City funds public defender organizations to provide legal defense to
immigrants arrested in the city—a service that people ICE arrests elsewhere
are not entitled to since immigration removal proceedings are civil
procedures.

But on occasion, detainees arrested in NYC and brought to OCJ have been moved
so quickly that public defense providers do not even become aware they were
there until after they’re already out of state, according to local advocates,
hampering their ability to actually provide representation.

Most advocates believe this bedlam to be strategic, helping the Trump
administration to make what is supposed to be civil, non-punitive detention
more punishing and exhausting in a bid to get people to just give up on their
cases and accept removal.

* * *

Orange County’s jail has been hampered by allegations of poor conditions
affecting detainees, particularly those arrested by ICE.

New York Lawyers for the Public Interest [published a
report](https://www.nylpi.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/English-OCJ-Health-
in-Detention-Report_FINAL.pdf) late last year based on reviewing medical
records of over a dozen of ICE detainees. They alleged a pattern of delayed,
inconsistent, and ineffectual medical care at the facility by both corrections
staff and outside medical contractors. The sheriff's office
[denied](https://radiocatskill.org/orange-county-sheriffs-office-calls-
medical-neglect-allegations-inside-jail-rumors/) the [validity of the
report](https://www.wamc.org/news/2026-04-24/sheriff-says-report-detailing-
medical-neglect-in-orange-county-jails-ice-unit-is-just-rumors) without
offering specifics, and stressed that many detainees had been accused of
“severe crimes.”

Genesis Ramos, the Democratic leader of the county legislature, told _Bolts_
that her office had followed up on these concerns but had not been able to
specifically substantiate them. “What we’ve been assured over and over again
is that the jail is subject to a lot of scrutiny and different audits,
different levels of certification that the jail has to go through,” she said.
“As a legislator, we only have but so much authority in terms of the data and
operations in the jail.”

Ramos added that she had visited the jail twice during her time as a local
legislator, and “never saw anything that was nefarious in nature or that was
alarming or concerning per se.” According to Samuel, though, staff would
repaint, clean, and provide better food whenever auditors or legislators would
visit. Samuel also complains of medical deficiencies. After he was diagnosed
with diabetes in jail, he said the food he was served remained the same and
his medical appointments kept being delayed; he is now concerned he may have
permanent vision problems.

The actual status of the ICE detainee population at the jail remains unclear.
Since the law barring local collaboration with ICE went into effect, detainees
were transferred out in large numbers, though some were only transferred after
the Aug. 25 date at which the county was required to exercise the termination
clause of its ICE contract.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/26149659968094-2400x1600.jpg)New York Governor Kathy
Hochul this spring after signing new legislation to protect people in New York
from overreach by ICE (photo by Michael Brochstein/Sipa USA via AP Images)

A large group of detainees was transferred to the Brooklyn Metropolitan
Detention Center, a federal prison, as part of the process to wind down the
ICE contract. According to McCoubrey’s tracking, detainees were also sent to
the GEO Group-run ICE facility in Jena, Louisiana, which is also where Mahmoud
Khalil was held for months; to the [deadly](https://www.theguardian.com/us-
news/2026/aug/13/immigrant-dies-delaney-hall-new-jersey) Delaney Hall in New
Jersey; to [the troubled Miami Correctional
Facility](https://indianacapitalchronicle.com/2026/07/30/ice-responds-after-
reports-of-medical-staffing-failures-at-prison-holding-immigration-detainees/)
in Indiana; and to other institutions in Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, and Texas.

But advocates at Envision and some public defenders say they caught wind of
additional book-ins after Aug. 25. Under state law, localities have until Nov.
25 to certify that they are in compliance, though receiving new detainees in
that interim period could arguably run afoul of it.

Johnson-Powers, of Envision, said the fund had received a call to its hotline
from an ICE detainee at OCJ as late as Sept. 15. The next day, James Potter,
the captain of the corrections division at the sheriff’s office,
[told](https://www.orangecountyny.gov/AgendaCenter/ViewFile/Minutes/_09162026-2841)
a meeting of the county legislature’s public safety committee that “the ICE
detainee count was 171 for August and as of this morning it was zero,” per
meeting minutes. Potter also noted year-to-date “boarder revenue,” i.e.,
income from renting jail beds to ICE, was $8.13 million.

In response to _Bolts_ ’ questions about the current ICE detainee population,
transfers, conditions at the jail, and compliance with state law, the sheriff
referred all questions to ICE, which did not respond.

The office of Orange County Executive Steve Neuhaus also did not respond to
multiple requests for comment. A spokesperson for New York Attorney General
Letitia James, who has the power to go after jurisdictions in noncompliance,
did not address specific questions about Orange County, but clarified that the
office views Nov. 25 as the compliance deadline.

* * *

If and when the jail stops housing ICE detainees, that doesn’t end the
conversation over immigration detention in the county. In late June, Project
Salt Box [reported](https://www.projectsaltbox.com/p/houston-firm-
wins-355-million-lease) that the federal government leased a massive warehouse
in Newburgh, a city in Orange County, with some indication that it could be
used for ICE detention, including the requirement that it have a sally port
large enough for detainee buses and vans.

The prospect has led to [significant community
pushback](https://radiocatskill.org/residents-push-for-answers-on-ice-
contract-in-newburgh/) this fall.

ICE detention is also a point of contention in November’s sheriff race between
Arteta and Rivers, a rematch of the 2022 election in which Arteta [easily
prevailed](https://www.chroniclenewspaper.com/home/arteta-beats-rivers-in-
orange-county-sheriff-race-NF2263852).

Rivers, the Democratic challenger, has criticized Arteta for signing on to the
lawsuit against the immigration legislation, arguing that the sheriff should
keep their focus local: “Orange County residents deserve a Sheriff who is
focused on their needs, not one chasing national headlines at the expense of
public trust,” he said in a [Facebook post in
August](https://www.facebook.com/BernieRiversforSheriff/posts/for-immediate-
releaseorange-county-sheriff-candidate-bernie-riverscriticizes-
she/1072151678534135/). He has also warned that the debates are set to
continue given the Newburgh warehouse, telling _Bolts_ that immigration
detention was a “hot-topic button… with the federal government for the second
time looking to purchase or lease facilities here in Orange County to house
ICE detainees.”  

“I’m not saying the federal government doesn’t have a right to enforce
immigration law; they have every right to enforce immigration law, but the way
they’re doing it is just wrong," he added.

Still, he doesn’t see himself as a “standard-bearer” for the anti-ICE movement
in the county. “It does come into the political conversation. People want to
talk about ICE,” he told _Bolts_. “I really didn’t want and don’t want to
focus the sheriff race totally on what’s going on in ICE.”

Rivers said he would still consider notifying ICE about detainees when
appropriate. But he could not immediately say when it would be, telling
_Bolts_ he’d look into the laws and regulations when in office. If elected,
Rivers also committed to looking into concerns over food and medical care at
OCJ, including for people held there on criminal charges.

But Rivers also lamented that the main reaction he was getting from would-be
voters was surprise that there was even an election for sheriff, a reality he
partly chalked up to the collapse of local media.

Several of the community organizations that participated in the Dignity Not
Detention coalition and pushed for the cancellation of the Orange County ICE
contract told _Bolts_ that they’re staying out of the race and had no comment
on it. Attention now is focused on support for those who are being moved out,
including the group sent to Brooklyn MDC, a federal facility housing roughly
1,400 people that was denounced by a judge [in
2024](https://www.nydailynews.com/2024/09/15/fed-prison-system-stops-sending-
newly-sentenced-inmates-to-notorious-mdc-brooklyn-jail/) for its “dangerous,
barbaric conditions.”  

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/26287164313915-2400x1920.jpg)A rally in front of the
Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn on Oct. 13, 2026 after Oscal Belgal
was shot by ICE agents and detained at MDC; the speaker is Public Advocate
Jumaane Williams (photo by Gabriele Holtermann/Sipa USA via AP Images).

“The levels of security and just degradation and lack of humanity through this
intense security, it’s just very different from being in a small county jail,”
said Johnson-Powers.

Still, even if the closure of OCJ to ICE detainees won’t address the broader
issues of an administration committed to mass deportation and armed with
[enormous funding](https://boltsmag.org/how-the-gop-megabill-would-
turbocharge-local-immigration-enforcement/), advocates say the law restricting
local cooperation with ICE and the contract’s cancellation have value.

McCoubrey, the advocate at Envision, stresses “the multiplier effect that
every ICE bed has,” telling _Bolts,_ “70,000 [total detention] beds is already
a scary number. But the fact that that facilitates hundreds and hundreds of
thousands of deportations every year really brings home the value of any
amount of any dent that you can make in local detention capacity.”
